albumTitle: Music Has the Right to Children
headline: A Past That Never Happened
standfirst: Two brothers, a studio in the Pentland Hills and a box of worn-out tape made one of the most quietly influential records of the 1990s. This is how *Music Has the Right to Children* learned to sound like a memory you never had.

sections.heading: A signal from the hills
paragraphs: Put the record on and the first thing you hear is not quite a song. [[Wildlife Analysis]] lasts barely more than a minute: a slow, wavering chord, a melody that seems to be remembering itself as it goes, a sound like a television left on in another room. Then it is gone, and something heavier starts to move. It is a strange way to open a debut album, and a perfect one, because *Music Has the Right to Children* never quite announces itself. It arrives the way an old memory does, sideways and already half dissolved.

The album came out on 20 April 1998, released in Britain jointly by Warp and the small Manchester label Skam, and in America by Matador. Its makers were two men from Scotland who called themselves Boards of Canada and who, at the time, gave the world almost nothing to go on. They were credited as Michael Sandison and Marcus Eoin. Few people knew that Eoin was Marcus's middle name, or that the pair were brothers. They kept that to themselves until 2005, saying later that they had simply wanted to avoid being compared with Orbital, the best-known sibling act in British electronic music.

What they did give away was the music, and it turned out to be enough. Nearly three decades on, this is one of the most loved electronic records ever made, a gold-certified fixture of best-of lists and a sound so widely absorbed that it can be hard to hear how odd it was in 1998. To hear it fresh, it helps to go back to where it came from: a childhood split between two countries, a pair of tape recorders, and a studio in the hills south-west of Edinburgh.

pullQuote.text: It arrives the way an old memory does, sideways and already half dissolved.

sections.heading: Two countries, one name
paragraphs: Michael Sandison was born in 1971 and Marcus in 1973, and they grew up in the north of Scotland in a house full of instruments and recording gear. Their father worked in construction, and his work took the family to Canada between 1979 and 1980, to Calgary. It was a short stay, but it left a mark. The brothers would later name their project after the National Film Board of Canada, the public body whose documentaries and animated films they had watched as children.

That choice says a great deal about the music that followed. The Film Board's work belonged to a particular kind of public culture: earnest, curious, made to educate, often beautiful almost by accident. Nature films, science films, portraits of communities, all scored with library music and narrated in calm, explanatory voices. For a child those films were simply what was on. Heard again as an adult, the same material carries a charge it never had at the time, a feeling of a world that was trying to teach you something and has since quietly disappeared.

The brothers were recording long before they were releasing. A 2005 interview with Clash describes them, at around ten years old, playing sounds on one tape machine and recording them on another across the air between the two, then swapping the tapes and doing it again to build up layers. It is a crude technique, and every pass adds hiss and blur. In hindsight it reads like a manifesto. The degradation was never a flaw to be cleaned up later. It was part of the sound from the very start.

pullQuote.text: The degradation was never a flaw to be cleaned up later.

sections.heading: Hexagon Sun
paragraphs: As teenagers the brothers lived in Balerno, a village on the edge of Edinburgh beside the Pentland Hills, and that landscape of moor, reservoir and sheep track became their base. Boards of Canada began as a band in 1986, with a changing cast of members, and over the following years shrank to a core of the two brothers and their friend Chris Horne. Around them grew a loose collective of musicians, artists and friends that came to be called Hexagon Sun, known for gatherings in the woods that the Clash interview describes as music and talk around a campfire in the open air.

Hexagon Sun was also the name of their studio, formally adopted in the summer of 1995. The press would later describe it as a bunker, an image that suited the mystery perfectly. In an interview around the album's release, the brothers brushed that off as the record label's exaggeration. In the Clash interview, Mike Sandison put the appeal more plainly: out in the country you can make as much noise as you like, nobody complains, and the outside world's fashions stay at a distance.

In those years the brothers released music in tiny numbers on their own label, Music70, mostly cassettes passed among friends and family. The first record to reach a wider public was *Twoism*, a self-financed EP issued in August 1995 in a run of roughly a hundred copies. It included an early form of [[Smokes Quantity]], which would surface again on the album with its loping beat and smeared, sun-warped melody intact. Copies of *Twoism* became so scarce that they changed hands for hundreds of pounds before Warp finally reissued it in 2002.

sections.heading: A tape in the post
paragraphs: The break came through the post. In 1996 the brothers finished a new EP, *Hi Scores*, and began sending it out to people whose music they admired. One copy reached Sean Booth of Autechre, who suggested they get in touch with Skam, the label that had put out Autechre's own early work. Skam released *Hi Scores* at the end of 1996. Among its six tracks was [[Turquoise Hexagon Sun]], whose title nods to the collective and whose slow, glassy chords and patient beat are as close to a statement of intent as Boards of Canada ever made. It would carry straight over onto the album.

Skam wanted a full-length record. So did Warp, the Sheffield label that had become the home of Aphex Twin, Autechre and much of the most adventurous electronic music in Britain. Rather than choose, the two labels agreed to release the album together. Before it arrived, Skam issued one more taster in January 1998: the *Aquarius* EP, whose title track would also find its way onto the album.

That summer, with the record out, the duo recorded a session for John Peel at the BBC's Maida Vale studios. It is a reminder of how the album first travelled, by late-night radio and word of mouth rather than by any great marketing push. The album's own chart history is modest to the point of comedy: number 193 on the UK albums chart, number 24 on the independent chart. The audience it eventually found came slowly, and then never left.

sections.heading: How a memory is built
paragraphs: *Music Has the Right to Children* was put together at Hexagon Sun between 1995 and 1997. The tools were not exotic: samplers, vintage synthesizers deliberately pulled out of tune, drum machines and reel-to-reel tape. What was unusual was the attitude. Where much electronic music of the time chased clarity and speed, Boards of Canada worked to make their sounds older, softer and less certain. In a 1998 interview with the French writers Ariel Kyrou and Jean-Yves Leloup, the brothers explained that they played both electronic and acoustic instruments on the record, then rebuilt the sounds electronically until their origins blurred.

You can hear the method everywhere. The synth lines on [[Roygbiv]], a title borrowed from the schoolroom mnemonic for the colours of the rainbow, wobble as if the tape were stretching under the melody. [[Sixtyten]] sets a darker, more insistent pattern turning beneath clouds of processed sound. Little sketches like [[Bocuma]] and [[Olson]] are barely more than a phrase and a texture, over in a minute or two, but they do as much as the long tracks to set the mood. They feel like fragments of film found at the end of a reel.

Underneath much of it is a beat that owes more to hip-hop than to the dancefloor. [[An Eagle In Your Mind]] and [[Telephasic Workshop]] move with the slow, heavy swing of a breakbeat played back at the wrong speed, and that physical weight keeps the album from floating away into ambient wallpaper. The brothers had little interest in the dance music fashionable at the time, and Mike Sandison later said it annoyed them to find their records filed in the dance section of big shops. The rhythms here are for nodding along on headphones, not for clubs.

One of the album's loveliest details happened by chance. While they were recording [[Rue the Whirl]], a studio window was left open and birdsong drifted onto the tape. Rather than redo the take, the brothers decided the birds made the track better and kept them. It is hard to think of a neater summary of the whole project: a studio in the hills, a machine-made groove, and the outside world allowed in to soften the edges.

pullQuote.text: They feel like fragments of film found at the end of a reel.

sections.heading: Voices from the classroom
paragraphs: The album is almost entirely instrumental, but it is full of voices. Most of them are children's, and many come from the world of educational television. Several samples are taken from *Sesame Street*, including those heard on [[The Color of the Fire]] and [[Aquarius]]. On the first, a single small voice sounds out a short phrase, slowed and looped until its warmth starts to feel slightly unreal. On the second, children's voices bounce across a fat, bright groove, and the effect is something like joy recorded through a wall.

The titles keep the schoolroom atmosphere going. [[Triangles & Rhombuses]] sounds like the heading of a geometry lesson. [[Telephasic Workshop]] could be an after-school club in some slightly sinister science-fiction town. The brothers described their titles in 1998 as cryptic references that listeners might or might not catch, many of them private, and it is wise to take them at their word rather than build theories on top. One reference, at least, is clear. [[Pete Standing Alone]] shares its name with the central figure of *Circle of the Sun*, a 1960 Film Board documentary by Colin Low about the Kainai Nation of southern Alberta, for which a young Kainai man named Pete Standing Alone provided the narration. The track itself is among the album's most spacious, long and unhurried.

Asked, around the time of their third album, how they approached memory in their music, the brothers spoke of building little melodic phrases that remind you of something you cannot quite place, and of corroding the sound itself. The aim, they said, was not to copy the past accurately but to be "inventing a past that didn't really happen". It is the key to why the album works on people who never saw a Film Board documentary in their lives. The memories it triggers are not yours, exactly. They are memories of a kind of childhood, played back on worn tape.

sections.heading: The faces that aren't there
paragraphs: The cover finishes the thought. It is an altered family holiday photograph, taken at Banff in the Canadian Rockies: a group of figures posed in the open air, the colours washed into a cold blue-green, and the faces wiped away. There is nothing frightening in the picture itself. It is the absence that unsettles, the sense of a snapshot that should be personal and has had the persons taken out. It is a family photo with room in it for anyone, which is exactly what the music is too.

That gentle unease runs right through the record. [[Kaini Industries]] lasts less than a minute and sounds like an old corporate jingle heard through fog. [[Open the Light]], late in the running order, glows warmly and drifts. And the album closes on [[One Very Important Thought]], a short, quiet piece in which a voice speaks over the music. After an hour of half-heard children and melodies like faded photographs, it lands as a final lesson from the classroom, one that leaves you not quite sure what you have just been taught.

Mike Sandison once said that in music, words are "a really low-res way of conveying ideas". It is a fitting line for a record that, for all its talking voices, never explains itself. The meaning sits in the tone of the chords and the wear on the tape, not in anything that could be written down.

pullQuote.text: It is a family photo with room in it for anyone, which is exactly what the music is too.

sections.heading: The long afterglow
paragraphs: The first reviews were warm. The Manchester Evening News called it the best album its readers would hear that year, and in the Daily Telegraph Alexis Petridis praised its warmth and humanity. Over time the praise grew into something closer to reverence. When the album was reissued in 2004, Pitchfork gave it a perfect score. The site later placed it second in its list of the greatest IDM albums and twenty-sixth among the best albums of the 1990s, and Mojo included it in its hundred modern classics. In 2025, more than a quarter of a century after it barely scraped into the charts, it was certified gold in the UK.

Some editions carry a bonus track, [[Happy Cycling]], included on the 1998 American release and the 2004 British reissue. The brothers had played it on that 1998 Peel session, and it is one of their most serene pieces: nearly eight minutes of easy, rolling motion that feels like the album exhaling after its last word.

The record's influence has been enormous and often indirect. Writers at Fact have traced its fingerprints through the work of Four Tet, Bibio, Gold Panda, Lone, Ulrich Schnauss, Tim Hecker and The Caretaker, and critics have heard it as a forerunner of the British hauntology of the following decade, music built from the half-remembered public culture of a vanished childhood. Its warped synths and dusty drums became a whole vocabulary, borrowed by bedroom producers, film composers and game soundtracks alike.

Yet nothing that followed quite replaced it, perhaps because the thing that makes it special is so hard to copy. The detuned synths and tape hiss are only tools. What Boards of Canada really made in those hills was a feeling: the ache of looking at a picture you know you are in, and not being able to find your own face. Play it again from [[Wildlife Analysis]] and the feeling is still there, waiting, exactly as unsettled and as tender as it was in 1998.

pullQuote.text: What Boards of Canada really made in those hills was a feeling.
